summary: Specifies a method for resolving IP addresses to HIPPI hardware addresses and for emulating IP broadcast in a logical IP subnet. It interoperates between HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 equipment. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers on a very fast cable need a way to find each other by name and shout to everyone at once. This explains how to do both on that kind of cable.

questions: how does arp work over hippi
how is ip broadcast emulated on hippi
subtitle: How computers on a HIPPI switch find each other's hardware addresses, and how IP broadcast is faked where the switch cannot do it.

tldr.problem: HIPPI switches are not required to support broadcast, so classic ARP cannot work on them, yet many networking protocols rely on broadcast.
tldr.mechanism: HARP, a two-phase adaptation of ARP and Inverse ARP, registers each port with a HARP server (or detects real broadcast) and then resolves IP addresses to HIPPI hardware addresses. The HARP server also acts as a PIBES that re-sends broadcast messages to every registered port.
tldr.outcome: IP over HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400 gets address resolution and an Ethernet-like broadcast service, but broadcast emulation is limited to light traffic and HARP messages are not authenticated.

today: RFC 2834 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1374 and is updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: Why HIPPI Needs Its Own ARP
sections.content:
The High-Performance Parallel Interface (HIPPI) is a dual simplex data channel that can send and receive at 800 or 1600 megabits per second. ANSI standards cover its framing, its switches and its encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC, but they stop short of describing HIPPI as a local area network. RFC 2067 describes how IP is encapsulated over HIPPI-800. This memo adds address resolution and IP broadcast emulation on top.

The RFC defines HARP, a method for resolving IP addresses to HIPPI hardware addresses, as an adaptation of ARP and Inverse ARP (RFC 2390). It is built to interoperate between HIPPI-800 and HIPPI-6400, also known as Gigabyte System Network (GSN). Together with RFC 2067 it obsoletes RFC 1374.

The motivation for broadcast emulation is practical: HIPPI switches are not required to implement broadcast, but many standard networking protocols rely on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast cables like HIPPI had no way to look up who is where, and no way to shout to everyone. This RFC adds both, so normal internet programs can work on them.

sections.title: Subnets, Addresses and the HRAL
sections.content:
HARP works inside a logical IP subnet (LIS). All members of a LIS share the same IP network or subnet address and mask. Several LISs can run over the same HIPPI network, and ports in different subnets SHOULD talk through an IP router even if a direct HIPPI connection would be possible.

A HIPPI hardware address combines a Switch Address (carried in the I-field, mapped by the switch to a physical port) with an optional 48-bit Universal LAN MAC Address (ULA). If there is no ULA, that field MUST be zero. The ULA is RECOMMENDED, and REQUIRED to interoperate with a conventional network.

Every port is configured with the same ordered HARP Request Address List (HRAL), with at least two entries. The first MUST be the broadcast address 0x07000FE1 FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. The second is REQUIRED to be the official HARP server address 0x07000FE0 00:00:00:00:00:00. Any further HARP servers follow, sorted in decreasing order of the 12-bit destination switch address.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone gets the same phone list. The first number is the loudspeaker and the second is the front desk. Extra front desks come after that.

sections.title: Registration and Operational Phases
sections.content:
HARP is a two-phase protocol. In the registration phase a port works out whether it is on broadcast-capable hardware, using the Inverse ARP style InHARP_REQUEST. It first sends one to the first HRAL address. If it sees its own request come back, the network supports broadcast, the rest of the HRAL is ignored and the broadcast entry is the authoritative HARP service.

If not, the port sends InHARP_REQUEST to the remaining HRAL entries. If it receives its own request at the second address, the port itself is the HARP server and MUST provide broadcast service through a PIBES. If it receives an InHARP_REPLY, it is a client. The authoritative service is the responsive server that appears first in the HRAL. On a non-broadcast network the client retries each non-broadcast server address at least once every 5 seconds until one of the termination criteria is met, and it stays registered with all HARP servers in the HRAL.

In the operational phase the client sends HARP_REQUEST messages to the authoritative address and learns from HARP_REPLY messages. This works the same on broadcast and non-broadcast networks. The authoritative server SHOULD be considered non-responsive if it misses a registration request or any two HARP_REQUESTs in the last 120 seconds. Registration then restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: First you check whether you can shout to the room. If you can, you do. If not, you sign in at the front desk. After that, whenever you need a room number, you ask the desk.

sections.title: Servers, Table Aging and Permanent Entries
sections.content:
A HARP server MUST accept HIPPI connections and expects an InHARP_REQUEST as the first message from a client. It records the IP address, switch address and ULA with a time stamp, and replies from its table: a HARP_REPLY or InHARP_REPLY if it has the answer, otherwise a HARP_NAK. A table of five cases (IP entry and hardware entry existing or new, linked or not) says how to link, unlink and create entries, for example when an IP alias moves to another interface. When mappings change, the server SHOULD use the PIBES to send HARP_REPLY messages to every hardware address in its table, shortening the time clients hold stale entries.

Aging MUST be supported because IP addresses and interfaces are likely to move. A client MUST invalidate an entry that ages beyond 15 minutes, and a server MUST delete an entry that ages beyond 20 minutes. On a non-broadcast network, a client MUST refresh its entry for the server at least once every 15 minutes. A client SHOULD revalidate an entry before it ages by sending a HARP_REQUEST. If the answer is a HARP_NAK the entry is removed, and if the server fails, the client tries an InHARP_REQUEST directly to the entry's hardware address.

Permanent entries are allowed so that legacy adapters with static ARP tables can interoperate. They are not aged, and the server SHOULD use them to answer requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk keeps a list of who lives where and crosses out names that have not checked in for a while. If a name is crossed out, you ask again before sending anything important.

sections.title: HARP Message Encoding
sections.content:
A HARP message rides inside HIPPI-FP and HIPPI-LE headers. The HIPPI-LE header carries Message_Type 0 for a data message, and both address types are set to 2, a 12-bit logical address. An IEEE 802.2 LLC header begins in the first byte of the D2_Area, with SSAP-DSAP-CTL 0xAA-AA-03 announcing a SNAP header. The SNAP header uses OUI 0x00-00-00 and the Ethertype 2054 (0x0806), the same for ARP, HARP and InHARP. The LLC/SNAP header is fixed at 8 bytes.

The HARP message uses the usual ARP fields. ar$hrd MUST be sent as 28 (HIPARP) and is accepted as 28, 1 or 6. ar$pro is 2048 for IP, and ar$pln is 4. For HIPPI-800 the hardware address is 10 bytes (switch address plus ULA), so the hardware length fields are 10. For HIPPI-6400 the hardware address is only the 6-byte ULA, so the length fields are 6, which tells the two versions apart.

A HARP_NAK is the received HARP_REQUEST copied byte for byte with only the operation code changed. HARP_NAK MUST be implemented. A client that receives an unsupported operation code MUST discard the message quietly and carry on.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a letter in an envelope in another envelope. The outer ones tell the switch where to send it, and the inner one holds the actual question, such as who has this IP address.

sections.title: Broadcast Emulation with PIBES
sections.content:
HIPPI-SC does not require switches to support broadcast. If a LIS does not have it, the HARP server MUST emulate it with a Protocol for an IP Broadcast Emulation Server (PIBES). The PIBES treats the HARP server's current table as its target list. It accepts only messages whose source is in that list and whose destination is an IP LIS broadcast address, a multicast address or 255.255.255.255, drops the rest, and forwards each valid message to every address in the list.

Running the PIBES on the same port as the HARP server is RECOMMENDED, because the memo does not define a protocol for exchanging the HARP table. HIPPI has no multicast mapping, so IP multicast is sent the same way as 255.255.255.255.

There is a built-in limit. In a LIS with n ports, the upper bound on broadcast bandwidth is (total bandwidth)/(n+1). This is fine for protocols such as RIP, OSPF and NIS, but it cannot carry high-bandwidth broadcast, which would need hardware support.
sections.plainLanguage: With no loudspeaker, the front desk takes your announcement and walks it to every room. That works for small notes but not for a marching band.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content:
HARP messages are not authenticated, which the RFC calls a potential flaw that could let corrupt information into the server system. It also notes the known issue of port impersonation through address resolution protocols and says no special security mechanism is added. It adds that not all security issues of ARP over HIPPI are clearly understood.

Left open for further study are the synchronization and coordination of multiple HARP servers and multiple broadcast servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write a fake note to the front desk, and nobody checks who really wrote it. The authors say so honestly.

messages.label: InHARP_REQUEST (op 8)
messages.note: Registers the client's address mapping with the server.

messages.label: InHARP_REPLY (op 9)
messages.note: Confirms registration and gives the server's IP address.

messages.label: HARP_REQUEST (op 1)
messages.note: Operational phase: asks for a target's hardware address.

messages.label: HARP_REPLY (op 2) or HARP_NAK (op 10)
messages.note: Answers from its table, or refuses if it has no entry.

items.label: HARP_REQUEST
items.desc: Asks for the hardware address of a target IP address.

items.label: InHARP_REQUEST
items.desc: Inverse request, used for registration and broadcast detection.

items.label: HARP_NAK
items.desc: Sent when the server cannot answer the request.
